unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coral Bay Berry Farm is a family-run business on the southern coast of Country X, growing strawberries and blueberries across 18 hectares. It employs 26 seasonal pickers and harvested 120 tonnes of fruit last year, selling to Country X supermarkets at an average of $4.20 per kilogram, earning about $504,000. The family reinvested $60,000 in refrigerated storage in January.

A refrigerated cargo flight route opened in March, cutting delivery to Country V from 9 days by sea to 14 hours by air. The owner, Elena Marchetti, has been offered contracts by three Country V supermarkets willing to pay $6.50 per kilogram for up to 30 tonnes a year, but air freight costs $1.40 per kilogram and Country V quality certificates cost $18,000 a year. Elena must decide whether to accept the export deal or stay with domestic sales.

questions.question_text: Define 'exports'.
questions.model_answer: Exports are goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in another country. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Goods and services produced in one country [1]
Sold to buyers in another country / sent abroad [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation has increased, using Coral Bay Berry Farm as context.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Improvements in transport make it possible to move goods quickly and safely across long distances. [k] The new refrigerated cargo flight has cut the delivery journey to Country V from 9 days by sea to 14 hours by air. [app] Reason 2: The growth of multinational supermarket chains creates demand for products across many countries. [k] Three Country V supermarkets have offered Elena $6.50 per kilogram, showing overseas buyers are actively seeking Country X fruit. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Improvements in transport allow goods to reach distant markets faster and more cheaply [1]
Growth of multinationals / global retailers creates cross-border demand [1]
application_max_2: Refrigerated cargo flight cut journey from 9 days by sea to 14 hours
Three Country V supermarkets offering $6.50 per kilogram for up to 30 tonnes a year

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities the export deal could create for Coral Bay Berry Farm.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting opens up a larger market and increases sales revenue. [k] The deal would add up to 30 tonnes a year at $6.50 per kilogram, about $195,000 of new revenue. [app] This extra income would help cover the $60,000 invested in refrigerated storage and lift profits. [an] Opportunity 2: Selling abroad spreads risk across different markets. [k] At present all 120 tonnes of fruit go to Country X supermarkets. [app] If domestic demand fell, sales to Country V would protect the farm's income and the jobs of its 26 seasonal pickers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Exporting opens access to new/larger markets raising revenue [1]
Selling into more than one market spreads risk [1]
application_max_2: 30 tonnes a year at $6.50 per kilogram is about $195,000 of new revenue
All 120 tonnes currently sold to Country X supermarkets
analysis_max_2: Extra revenue helps cover the $60,000 storage investment and raises profit
Spreading sales across markets protects income and the 26 pickers' jobs if Country X demand falls

questions.question_text: Do you think Elena should accept the Country V export deal? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the deal would open a high-value market. [k] Three Country V supermarkets are offering $6.50 per kilogram, which is $2.30 above the $4.20 domestic average. [app] After $1.40 per kilogram freight, Elena would still net more per kilogram, raising total revenue and spreading the farm's risk beyond Country X. [an] However, exports bring significant extra costs. [k] Freight on 30 tonnes costs $42,000 a year and Country V certificates cost $18,000 a year, so the gain over selling those 30 tonnes domestically is only about $9,000 a year. [app] Complex paperwork, tight flight schedules and currency changes could turn this slim margin into a loss, and cash tied up in certificates may be needed for months. [an] Overall, Elena should accept the export deal only if she is confident in freight reliability and certification, because the $9,000 annual gain is modest but proves access to Country V's much larger market. [eval] On balance, the strategic value of an established export channel outweighs the small price-premium risk, provided she does not divert more than 30 tonnes from her domestic customers. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Access to new markets can increase revenue and spread risk [1]
Exporting involves extra costs, risk and complexity [1]
application_max_2: $6.50 per kilogram offered vs $4.20 domestic average; about $9,000 extra a year after $42,000 freight and $18,000 certificates
Domestic revenue already about $504,000 from 120 tonnes; export route covers up to 30 tonnes
analysis_max_2: Higher net price per kilogram could raise profit and help recover the $60,000 storage investment
Freight, certificate and currency risks could erase the slim margin; diverting supply could strain domestic supermarket relationships
evaluation_max_2: Accept conditionally / with safeguards on freight and certification
Weighs small short-term gain against long-term access to the larger Country V market

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ridgeway & Grey Design Studio is a two-partner interior design partnership in Country X, trading for 6 years. It employs 4 designers and completes around 30 residential projects a year at an average fee of $9,800, generating roughly $294,000 a year. Until recently, every client was local and weekends were busy with site visits.

In the last 18 months, fast internet, video conferencing and cloud file sharing have allowed the studio to win clients in Country T and Country N without travelling. International jobs pay an average fee of $13,700, roughly 40% higher than domestic work, but the 5-hour time difference means late-evening calls. One partner wants to hire 2 more designers and chase overseas work full time; the other prefers to keep the studio small and serve Country X.

questions.question_text: Define 'globalisation'.
questions.model_answer: Globalisation is the process by which countries and their businesses become increasingly connected and interdependent through trade, technology, communication and investment. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Process of countries becoming more interconnected/integrated [1]
Driven by trade, technology and communication links [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation has allowed small businesses like Ridgeway & Grey to sell abroad.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Improvements in communication technology allow instant, cheap contact with customers anywhere. [k] Video conferencing and cloud file sharing let the studio win Country T and Country N clients without travelling. [app] Reason 2: The internet lets small businesses market themselves to a worldwide audience from one location. [k] Clients in Country T and Country N now commission projects remotely, with international fees averaging $13,700. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Improvements in communication technology reduce distance barriers [1]
The internet enables small firms to reach worldwide customers cheaply [1]
application_max_2: Video conferencing and cloud file sharing allowed Country T and Country N clients to be won without travel
International jobs pay an average fee of $13,700

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of globalisation for Ridgeway & Grey Design Studio.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: Access to global clients increases potential sales and revenue. [k] International jobs pay an average fee of $13,700, compared with $9,800 for domestic work. [app] Higher fees mean the same working time generates more income, lifting the studio's annual revenue above the current $294,000. [an] Benefit 2: Working internationally builds skills and reputation. [k] Meeting Country T and Country N standards pushes the 4 designers to raise quality and speed. [app] A stronger portfolio would attract more high-fee clients and deepen the partnership's competitive advantage. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Access to global markets increases sales/revenue potential [1]
International exposure improves skills and reputation [1]
application_max_2: International fees average $13,700 vs $9,800 domestic
Country T and Country N clients commissioned remotely / overseas work chased full time
analysis_max_2: Higher fee per project lifts revenue above $294,000 without new premises
Stronger portfolio and reputation attract further high-fee clients over time

questions.question_text: Do you think the studio should expand its international client work? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Expanding overseas would raise revenue and profit. [k] Country T and Country N projects pay about $13,700 each, roughly 40% more than the $9,800 domestic average, and those clients arrived at no extra marketing cost. [app] Hiring 2 extra designers could let the studio handle more high-fee work at once, lifting total income above the $294,000 earned last year. [an] However, overseas work brings strain and risk. [k] The 5-hour time difference means late-evening calls for the partners and the 4 existing designers. [app] Currency swings, late payment and possible quality slips could erase the 40% fee premium, and shrinking focus on Country X could starve the domestic base that currently fills the studio's workload. [an] Overall, the partnership should expand international work gradually, hiring one designer first and capping new overseas projects until routines settle. [eval] On balance, the higher international fees and word-of-mouth pipeline justify careful expansion rather than an all-out push into overseas work. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Access to global clients can increase revenue and profit [1]
Overseas expansion brings operational strain and currency/payment risk [1]
application_max_2: $13,700 average international fee vs $9,800 domestic (roughly 40% higher)
5-hour time difference forcing late-evening calls; current revenue roughly $294,000 with 4 designers
analysis_max_2: More fee income per project and capacity with 2 extra designers could lift revenue well above $294,000
Time-zone strain, currency risk and diluted local focus could wipe out the fee premium
evaluation_max_2: Expand gradually/conditionally with staged hiring
Weighs fee premium against wellbeing, quality and currency risks

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Dunwick Cannery Co is a private limited company in Country X, packing canned mangoes and peaches for 11 years. It employs 74 workers, processes around 2,600 tonnes of fruit a year and recorded revenue of $3.1 million last year, with a profit margin of 9%. Sales are almost all to Country X supermarkets under two long-standing contracts.

On 1 June, Country X and Country T abolished the 18% tariff on canned fruit under their new free trade agreement. Country T has 60 million consumers importing 40,000 tonnes of canned fruit a year. Two Country T importers offered Dunwick contracts worth $900,000 a year if it meets Country T safety standards, with certification costing $220,000. The board must choose between accepting the export contract and building a second production line for the domestic market.

questions.question_text: Define 'free trade'.
questions.model_answer: Free trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries without restrictions such as tariffs or quotas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: International trade without restrictions [1]
No tariffs or quotas between trading partners [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two ways in which the new free trade agreement could benefit Dunwick Cannery Co.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing tariffs makes exported goods cheaper and more competitive in foreign markets. [k] The abolition of the 18% tariff allows Dunwick's canned fruit to compete with Country T suppliers on price. [app] Reason 2: Free trade agreements open access to much larger markets. [k] Country T has 60 million consumers importing 40,000 tonnes of canned fruit a year, far bigger than Country X demand. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Removing tariffs makes exports more price-competitive [1]
Free trade agreements open access to larger foreign markets [1]
application_max_2: 18% tariff on canned fruit abolished on 1 June under the free trade agreement
Country T has 60 million consumers importing 40,000 tonnes a year

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for Dunwick Cannery Co of accepting the Country T export contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The contract creates a reliable new source of revenue. [k] The two Country T importers offer $900,000 a year, around 29% of last year's $3.1 million revenue. [app] This predictable income would cover the $220,000 certification cost within months and improve cash flow. [an] Benefit 2: Exporting diversifies the customer base and spreads risk. [k] Almost all sales currently go to Country X supermarkets under two long-standing contracts. [app] Adding Country T buyers reduces the danger that losing one domestic contract would seriously damage the business and its 74 workers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Export contracts provide predictable revenue stream [1]
Diversifying customers spreads risk [1]
application_max_2: $900,000 a year offered, about 29% of last year's $3.1 million revenue
Almost all sales currently to Country X supermarkets under two long-standing contracts
analysis_max_2: Predictable income covers the $220,000 certification within months and eases cash flow
Less dependence on two domestic contracts protects the business and its 74 workers

questions.question_text: Do you think Dunwick should accept the Country T export contract? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting the contract would lift revenue and profit. [k] The importers offer $900,000 a year, about 29% on top of last year's $3.1 million, helped by the 18% tariff saving. [app] Spreading sales across two countries would protect the 74 workers and reduce dependence on two domestic supermarket contracts. [an] However, the export route carries real costs. [k] Country T safety certification costs $220,000 and the contract depends on passing audits and meeting strict standards. [app] Building a second domestic production line would serve proven local demand with more certainty, and exchange-rate swings or importer failure could make the export deal less profitable than planned. [an] Overall, Dunwick should accept the export contract because Country T imports 40,000 tonnes a year and the $900,000 revenue would repay the $220,000 certification quickly. [eval] On balance, the strategic gain of an established Country T presence outweighs the safer second line, provided payment terms are agreed up front. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Export contracts can raise revenue and reduce dependence on one market [1]
Exporting involves certification, compliance and currency risk [1]
application_max_2: $900,000 a year offer (about 29% on $3.1 million) with 18% tariff removed
$220,000 certification cost vs building a second domestic production line
analysis_max_2: Diversified revenue protects 74 workers and reduces reliance on two domestic contracts
Certification, audit and exchange-rate risks could erode the deal's returns vs the safer domestic line
evaluation_max_2: Accept the export contract (justified choice)
Weighs strategic Country T presence against certainty of domestic expansion

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Emberglaze Sauce Co is a sole trader business making small-batch chilli sauce in Country X, founded 2 years ago by owner Priya Nandakumar in a rented unit. It employs 5 staff and produced 60,000 bottles last year at $6.50 each, generating $390,000 in revenue. Sales were flat until a cooking video Priya posted online was viewed 4.8 million times.

Distributors in Country N and Country R have since offered to stock Emberglaze in 400 shops, and the company website now takes orders from 30 countries through a global delivery firm. Foreign retailers pay after 60 days, copycat sauces have appeared abroad, and shipping glass bottles costs $1.10 each. Priya must decide whether to focus on exporting or grow her sales in Country X supermarkets first.

questions.question_text: Identify two reasons why globalisation has increased.
questions.model_answer: Improvements in transport, such as faster flights, container shipping and refrigerated delivery, allow goods to move around the world more quickly and cheaply. [1] The internet and global media, such as online video and social media, enable even very small businesses to reach customers worldwide at very low cost. [1] (Other valid answers include: removal of trade barriers; growth of multinational companies.)

knowledge_max_2: Transport improvements enabling faster/cheaper movement of goods [1]
Communication and internet/global media enabling worldwide reach [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why globalisation has helped a small business like Emberglaze reach foreign customers.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Global media can give small firms worldwide exposure at almost no cost. [k] One cooking video posted by Priya was viewed 4.8 million times, creating instant global awareness of the brand. [app] Reason 2: The internet allows businesses to sell directly to customers in other countries. [k] The website now takes orders from 30 countries through a global delivery firm. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Global media/social media provide cheap worldwide exposure [1]
Internet enables direct selling across borders without foreign offices [1]
application_max_2: Cooking video posted by Emberglaze viewed 4.8 million times, creating instant global awareness
Website takes orders from 30 countries via a global delivery firm

questions.question_text: Explain two opportunities exporting creates for Emberglaze Sauce Co.
questions.model_answer: Opportunity 1: Exporting dramatically increases the potential customer base. [k] Distributors in Country N and Country R have offered to stock Emberglaze in 400 shops abroad. [app] Covering 400 shops would spread fixed costs over far more bottles and lift profits. [an] Opportunity 2: Exporting early builds a defensible brand position. [k] Copycat sauces have already appeared in foreign markets since the video went viral. [app] Establishing Emberglaze first would make it harder for imitators to capture the overseas market. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Exporting opens far larger markets / customer base [1]
Early entry builds brand position ahead of rivals [1]
application_max_2: Distributors in Country N and Country R offering stock in 400 shops
Copycat sauces already appearing in foreign markets after the viral video
analysis_max_2: 400 shops spread fixed costs over more bottles, improving margins and profit
First-mover advantage makes it harder for copycat brands to gain distribution

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya should make exporting Emberglaze's main focus? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Exporting could transform Emberglaze's growth. [k] The distributor offers would place the sauce in 400 shops across Country N and Country R, and the website already ships to 30 countries. [app] Export sales would spread risk beyond Country X and drive the economies of scale needed to keep margins healthy. [an] However, exports create cash-flow and cost risks. [k] Foreign retailers pay after 60 days while production and shipping must be funded immediately. [app] At $1.10 per bottle for shipping plus copycat competition, margins could be squeezed, and focusing on Country X supermarkets first would be simpler, with faster payment and stronger local control. [an] Overall, Priya should pursue exports in a controlled way, signing one distributor at a time with tightened payment terms rather than rushing into 400 shops at once. [eval] On balance, the worldwide demand proven by the video makes exporting the bigger prize, provided cash flow and brand protection are managed carefully. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Exporting can scale a business and spread market risk [1]
Exporting brings working capital, shipping and competition risks [1]
application_max_2: 400 shops offered in Country N and Country R; website already ships to 30 countries
$1.10 per bottle shipping, 60-day payment terms and copycat sauces abroad
analysis_max_2: Larger volume spreads fixed costs and risk, enabling economies of scale
Delayed payment and shipping costs strain cash flow and could wipe out margins
evaluation_max_2: Phased/conditional export strategy rather than all at once
Weighs global opportunity shown by the video against cash-flow and brand risks

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Meadowlark Clothing is a private limited company running 9 clothing shops in Country X, trading for 8 years. It employs 120 staff and made revenue of $7.4 million last year selling mid-priced family fashion. Its own-brand dresses sell well, though Saturdays are the busiest days. All stock is designed in-house and bought from factories in Country X and Country Y.

A foreign online retailer, selling imported clothing 25% below Meadowlark's prices, now delivers to Country X in 3 days and advertises heavily on social media. Meadowlark's sales fell 12% last year and 2 of its 9 shops lost money. The directors are considering launching their own online store to sell across the region and halve delivery times, but building the website and delivery system would cost $400,000.

questions.question_text: Define 'imports'.
questions.model_answer: Imports are goods and services bought from other countries and brought into the home country for sale or use. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Goods and services bought from abroad [1]
Brought into the home country for sale or use [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two threats that globalisation poses to Meadowlark Clothing.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Foreign competitors can enter the home market and undercut local prices. [k] The foreign online retailer sells imported clothing 25% below Meadowlark's prices. [app] Reason 2: Global media and the internet make it easy for overseas rivals to reach local customers. [k] The retailer advertises heavily on social media, targeting Meadowlark's own customer base directly. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Foreign rivals can enter home markets and undercut local prices [1]
Internet and global media let overseas firms market directly to local consumers [1]
application_max_2: Foreign online retailer sells imported clothing 25% below Meadowlark's prices
Social media advertising reaches Meadowlark's customers, with sales down 12% last year

questions.question_text: Explain two ways Meadowlark could respond to the threat from foreign online retailers.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Launching its own online store could open regional markets beyond Country X. [k] Selling online lets a business reach customers in many countries from one base. [app] Spreading the $400,000 website and delivery cost over a much larger customer base would lift sales above the $7.4 million made last year. [an] Point 2: Meadowlark could differentiate on service and local knowledge. [k] Local shops offer fitting, easy returns and personal styling advice the online rival cannot match. [app] Retaining loyal customers through service would defend the 9 shops' sales despite cheaper imports. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Selling online can open wider regional/international markets [1]
Differentiating on service/local strengths defends share [1]
application_max_2: $400,000 to build website and delivery system to sell across the region
9 shops compete with a foreign retailer selling imported clothing 25% cheaper
analysis_max_2: Larger customer base spreads the $400,000 cost and rebuilds sales above $7.4 million
Service and fitting advantages keep loyal customers despite cheaper online imports

questions.question_text: Do you think Meadowlark should launch its own regional online store? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Launching an online store would let Meadowlark compete with foreign rivals directly. [k] A regional store could win back customers lost to the 25%-cheaper online retailer and sell beyond Country X. [app] If it recovers even part of the 12% sales decline, the $400,000 investment would spread fixed costs further and rebuild margins. [an] However, the investment is risky. [k] The $400,000 cost is large for a business whose sales fell 12% last year, with 2 of its 9 shops loss-making. [app] Matching a global giant on price and delivery is unlikely to succeed, and the money might protect existing revenue better if spent on improving shops and customer service. [an] Overall, Meadowlark should launch the online store modestly, starting with Country X delivery and adding regional reach only once order volumes cover costs. [eval] On balance, having an online channel is now essential for survival, but spending should be staged and tied to clear sales targets. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: An online channel lets a firm reach wider markets and compete with rivals [1]
Large investments carry financial risk for weaker firms [1]
application_max_2: $400,000 cost vs sales down 12% last year and 2 of 9 shops loss-making
Competitor sells imported clothing 25% below Meadowlark's prices with 3-day delivery
analysis_max_2: Recovering part of the 12% sales decline would spread costs and rebuild margins
Spending on shops and service may protect the safer existing $7.4 million revenue base
evaluation_max_2: Stage the launch / phased investment with clear targets
Weighs necessity of an online channel against financial risk and alternative uses of funds

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Velmont Electronics Plc is a multinational company assembling tablets and smartphones in 12 countries, trading for 26 years. In Country X it has proposed a $14 million factory to build tablets, employing 350 workers at wages 15% above the local minimum. It would pay corporation tax of about $2.2 million a year and use local component suppliers, but its profits would largely return to its home country.

Country X's industrial town of Brindleford lost its steel mill in 2019 and unemployment stands at 11%. The town council supports welcoming Velmont, offering a 10-year tax break worth $1.5 million, but residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training. Local rival Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to Velmont's higher wages.

questions.question_text: Define 'multinational company'.
questions.model_answer: A multinational company is a business that operates in more than one country, usually with headquarters in one country and branches, factories or offices overseas. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A business operating in more than one country [1]
Head office in one country with bases/factories overseas [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits a multinational company can bring to a host country.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Multinationals create employment in host countries. [k] Velmont's factory would employ 350 workers in Brindleford, where unemployment stands at 11%. [app] Reason 2: Multinationals bring capital investment and tax revenue. [k] The $14 million factory would pay about $2.2 million a year in corporation tax and buy from local suppliers. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals create jobs in host countries [1]
Multinationals bring investment and tax revenue / use of local suppliers [1]
application_max_2: 350 workers employed in Brindleford where unemployment stands at 11%
$14 million factory paying about $2.2 million a year corporation tax

questions.question_text: Explain two drawbacks for Brindleford of welcoming Velmont's factory.
questions.model_answer: Drawback 1: The factory may harm existing local employers. [k] Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to Velmont's higher wages. [app] Losing skilled staff could force Darrow to cut output or close, reducing competition and choice in Country X. [an] Drawback 2: The factory may impose costs on the local community. [k] Residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training. [app] These negative effects would fall on the community while most profits return to Velmont's home country, so some wealth would leave Brindleford. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals can damage local rival firms competing for scarce labour [1]
Multinationals can impose negative effects on the local community/environment [1]
application_max_2: Darrow Components, employing 90 people, fears losing workers to 15% above minimum wages
Residents fear traffic, noise and low-paid assembly work with little training
analysis_max_2: Losing skilled workers could bankrupt Darrow, reducing local competition and choice
Community bears external costs while profits flow abroad, weakening net benefit

questions.question_text: Do you think Country X should encourage Velmont to build its factory in Brindleford? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Welcoming Velmont would deliver major economic benefits. [k] The $14 million factory would employ 350 workers and pay about $2.2 million a year in corporation tax, reviving a town with 11% unemployment. [app] Local suppliers could win steady orders, and the $1.5 million 10-year tax break costs less than one year of tax revenue. [an] However, the factory also imposes real costs. [k] Most profits would return to Velmont's home country rather than stay in Country X. [app] Traffic and noise would burden residents, assembly roles offer little training, and Darrow Components risks losing staff from its 90-strong workforce, weakening an existing Country X business. [an] Overall, Country X should welcome Velmont with conditions, such as guaranteed apprenticeships and traffic limits, rather than an unconditional commitment. [eval] On balance, the jobs and tax revenue for a town with 11% unemployment outweigh the drawbacks if firm commitments are negotiated before approval. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals bring jobs, investment and tax revenue [1]
Multinationals take profits abroad and can harm local firms/communities [1]
application_max_2: $14 million factory; 350 jobs; about $2.2 million a year corporation tax in a town with 11% unemployment
10-year tax break worth $1.5 million; Darrow Components employing 90 fears staff losses
analysis_max_2: Jobs for 350 workers plus supplier orders and tax revenue would regenerate Brindleford's economy
Profit outflow, community external costs and harm to Darrow could reduce or outweigh net local gains
evaluation_max_2: Conditional welcome with negotiated safeguards (training, traffic limits)
Weighs regeneration and tax revenue against profit outflow, community costs and harm to local business

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eastvale Bicycle Works is a private limited company assembling electric bicycles in Country X, founded 9 years ago. It employs 140 workers and produced 28,000 e-bikes last year, selling 70% abroad, with revenue of $11.2 million. Rising Country X wages and energy costs have pushed its production cost to $290 per bike, while rivals in Country Q make bikes for $230.

Country Q, a host country keen to attract foreign firms, offers Eastvale a 10-year tax holiday, wages one-third lower, and a $2 million grant. Moving would cut production cost by $60 per bike, but closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant and Country X buyers would face about $9 extra per bike in shipping. The board must decide whether to relocate or stay at home.

questions.question_text: Define 'host country'.
questions.model_answer: A host country is a country in which a foreign-owned business establishes operations, such as a factory, while ownership remains based elsewhere. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Country where a foreign firm operates [1]
Firm remains owned from abroad / overseas head office [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why a business might locate in a host country such as Country Q.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Host countries often offer lower labour and production costs. [k] Country Q's wages are one-third lower, cutting Eastvale's cost from $290 to about $230 per bike. [app] Reason 2: Host governments often offer financial incentives to attract foreign firms. [k] Country Q is offering a 10-year tax holiday and a $2 million grant for setting up there. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Lower labour/production costs in some host countries [1]
Host governments offer incentives such as tax breaks and grants [1]
application_max_2: Country Q wages one-third lower, cutting cost from $290 to about $230 per bike
10-year tax holiday and a $2 million grant offered to attract Eastvale

questions.question_text: Explain two impacts on stakeholders if Eastvale relocates to Country Q.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Country X employees would lose their jobs. [k] Closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant. [app] Lost wages and skills would harm families and cut spending at local shops, damaging the wider community. [an] Point 2: Country X customers would pay more for their bikes. [k] Shipping from Country Q would add about $9 per bike. [app] Some buyers may switch to rival brands, cutting Eastvale's home-market sales and damaging its reputation. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Relocation can make the existing workforce redundant [1]
Customers face extra costs such as shipping from abroad [1]
application_max_2: Closing the Country X factory would make 140 workers redundant
Country X buyers would pay about $9 extra per bike in shipping
analysis_max_2: Redundancies harm household incomes, local spending and the factory town's economy
Higher prices may push customers to rivals, eroding home-market share and reputation

questions.question_text: Do you think Eastvale should relocate its factory to Country Q? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Relocating would make Eastvale far more competitive. [k] The move cuts production cost by $60 per bike, from $290 to $230, saving roughly $1.68 million a year on 28,000 bikes, before the $2 million grant. [app] Lower costs would protect the 70% of output sold abroad on $11.2 million revenue and keep Eastvale ahead of rivals. [an] However, relocation carries heavy costs for stakeholders. [k] 140 skilled Country X workers would lose their jobs, damaging morale and the company's local reputation. [app] Country X buyers would pay about $9 extra per bike, severance pay would be owed, and moving plant and staff could take a year, so savings would not be immediate. [an] Overall, Eastvale should relocate only after exhausting home-efficiency options, since losing 140 workers and its domestic base is hard to reverse. [eval] On balance, the $1.68 million annual saving strongly favours moving in the long run, but the board must price in redundancy and transition costs before deciding. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Relocation can cut costs and improve competitiveness [1]
Relocation harms existing workers, customers and the firm's reputation [1]
application_max_2: $60 saving per bike on 28,000 bikes (about $1.68 million a year) from $290 to $230
140 redundancies; $9 extra per bike for Country X buyers; $2 million grant and 10-year tax holiday
analysis_max_2: Savings plus incentives protect 70% overseas sales on $11.2 million revenue against rivals
Redundancy, severance, transition costs and higher customer prices could offset early savings
evaluation_max_2: Relocate only after exhausting domestic efficiency savings
Weighs long-run competitiveness against stakeholder harm and transition costs

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Northharbour Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in the port city of Northharbour, Country X, roasting coffee since 2011. It employs 32 staff and roasts 240 tonnes of beans a year, selling at $14 per kilogram to cafés and shops, generating about $3.36 million a year. Most beans are imported green from Country W.

In January the Country X government abolished the 15% import tariff on green coffee beans, fulfilling a free trade agreement with Country W. Northharbour's bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year. However, the same deal lets Country W's larger roasters sell into Country X at only 8% above Northharbour's prices, and two Country W brands have already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets. The directors must decide how to respond.

questions.question_text: Define 'trade barrier'.
questions.model_answer: A trade barrier is any government-imposed restriction on international trade, such as a tariff, quota or import licence, usually intended to protect domestic firms. [2].

knowledge_max_2: Government-imposed restriction on trade [1]
Examples: tariffs, quotas, import licences [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the removal of trade barriers encourages globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Removing tariffs makes imported goods cheaper and more competitive. [k] Northharbour's bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram once the 15% tariff was abolished, saving about $192,000 a year. [app] Reason 2: Free trade agreements open markets to businesses from partner countries. [k] The Country X–Country W deal has let larger Country W roasters sell into Country X supermarkets. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Removing tariffs lowers import prices and increases competitiveness [1]
Free trade agreements open markets between partner countries [1]
application_max_2: 15% import tariff abolished; bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year
Country W roasters now selling into Country X under the free trade agreement

questions.question_text: Explain two threats that the tariff removal creates for Northharbour Coffee Roasters.
questions.model_answer: Threat 1: Foreign competitors can now enter Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can sell into Country X at only 8% above Northharbour's prices. [app] Their scale lets them undercut on supermarket shelves, threatening Northharbour's sales to cafés and shops. [an] Threat 2: Competition may force Northharbour to cut its prices. [k] Two Country W brands have already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets. [app] If Northharbour matches lower prices, the $192,000 bean saving could be swallowed by a reduced margin on its $14 per kilogram coffee. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Foreign competitors can enter the home market after tariffs fall [1]
Greater rivalry puts downward pressure on price and margin [1]
application_max_2: Country W roasters can sell at only 8% above Northharbour's prices
Two Country W brands already taken shelf space in Country X supermarkets
analysis_max_2: Under-cutting at 8% or less erodes Northharbour's shelf position and café/shop sales
Price matching would absorb the $192,000 saving into a lower margin on $14 coffee

questions.question_text: Do you think the tariff removal will benefit Northharbour Coffee Roasters overall? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The tariff removal gives Northharbour a genuine cost advantage. [k] Bean costs fell from $5.20 to $4.40 per kilogram, saving about $192,000 a year across 240 tonnes. [app] Northharbour can hold prices steady, protect its 32 staff and reinvest the saving in quality and promotion. [an] However, the same agreement threatens Northharbour's home market. [k] Country W's larger roasters can now undercut within 8% of Northharbour's prices, and two Country W brands already occupy supermarket shelves. [app] If forced to match lower prices, the $192,000 saving could be wiped out, and Northharbour cannot match rivals' national advertising budgets. [an] Overall, Northharbour should use the saving to differentiate, such as launching speciality single-origin roasts that mass-market foreign brands cannot easily copy. [eval] On balance, the $192,000 annual saving is real but temporary, so long-term success depends on defending loyal café customers and a distinctive quality niche. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Tariff removal cuts input costs, helping margins [1]
Tariff removal also admits foreign competitors to the home market [1]
application_max_2: Bean costs down $5.20 to $4.40, saving about $192,000 a year on 240 tonnes
Country W brands undercut within 8% and hold supermarket shelf space; current revenue about $3.36 million
analysis_max_2: Saving can fund promotion, protect 32 jobs and defend price positioning
Price war could consume the saving and erode Northharbour's share against bigger rivals
evaluation_max_2: Use the saving to differentiate into speciality/quality niches
Weighs cost benefit against competitive threat and limited marketing resources

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Oxmoor Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Country X making solid-oak dining furniture. It employs 85 workers at one factory and produced 4,200 dining sets last year at $950 each, earning about $3.99 million. Most sales come through 6 independent shops and growth has slowed this year.

A multinational retailer from Country Z, Furniture World, opened its first 20 Country X stores in August at prices about 20% below Oxmoor's, forcing two local furniture shops to close. A trade body now offers Oxmoor a place in an export co-operative, 'Country X Living', sharing a $500,000 marketing budget at 3 European trade fairs, with members paying $30,000 each. Oxmoor must decide whether to join the co-operative or fight for share at home.

questions.question_text: Outline two reasons why the growth of multinational companies has increased globalisation.
questions.model_answer: Multinationals operate in many countries, linking markets and spreading products and brands across borders. [1] Multinationals encourage international trade and investment, making national economies more interdependent. [1]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals operate across multiple countries / link markets [1]
Multinationals encourage international trade and investment / interdependence [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two threats the entry of Furniture World poses to Oxmoor Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Multinational entrants use economies of scale to undercut local prices. [k] Furniture World opened 20 Country X stores at prices about 20% below Oxmoor's $950 sets, forcing two local furniture shops to close. [app] Reason 2: A large foreign retailer can capture market share rapidly through distribution power. [k] Its 20 stores give it instant national distribution that Oxmoor, relying on 6 independent shops, cannot match. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals undercut local prices using economies of scale [1]
Large foreign firms gain share quickly through distribution strength [1]
application_max_2: Furniture World opened 20 Country X stores at about 20% below Oxmoor's $950 sets, closing two local shops
Oxmoor relies on 6 independent shops for most of its $3.99 million sales

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of Oxmoor joining the 'Country X Living' export co-operative.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: The co-operative spreads export marketing costs across members. [k] 'Country X Living' combines a $500,000 campaign promoted at 3 European trade fairs and overseas websites. [app] For $30,000 a share, Oxmoor accesses promotional scale it could never achieve alone. [an] Benefit 2: Selling abroad diversifies Oxmoor's markets. [k] European trade fairs would reach buyers beyond Country X, unlike the 6 independent shops it relies on now. [app] Export sales would reduce dependence on a home market squeezed by Furniture World, protecting future revenue. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Co-operatives share marketing costs, making export viable for small firms [1]
Diversifying into export markets spreads risk [1]
application_max_2: $500,000 budget shared at 3 European trade fairs and overseas websites for a $30,000 member fee
Oxmoor currently sells mainly through 6 independent shops in Country X
analysis_max_2: Shared budget gives Oxmoor reach far beyond what $30,000 alone could buy
Export sales reduce exposure to Furniture World's undercutting at home

questions.question_text: Do you think Oxmoor should join the 'Country X Living' export co-operative? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Joining the co-operative would defend Oxmoor against multinational competition. [k] Furniture World sells at about 20% below Oxmoor's $950 price and has already forced two local furniture shops to close. [app] For $30,000, Oxmoor would access a $500,000 marketing programme and buyers at 3 European trade fairs, potentially lifting output above the current 4,200 dining sets a year. [an] However, exporting through the co-operative is demanding and uncertain. [k] Oxmoor must meet overseas standards, handle shipping and currency risk, and pay $30,000 before any return materialises. [app] With only 85 workers, splitting production between domestic and export orders could strain quality, and weak trade-fair turnout would waste the fee entirely. [an] Overall, Oxmoor should join the co-operative, because its home market is shrinking under multinational pressure and the shared budget makes export realistic. [eval] On balance, the $30,000 stake is modest against the threat to its $3.99 million revenue, provided quality and cash flow are protected during the transition. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Export co-operatives help small firms reach overseas markets [1]
Exporting carries standards, shipping, currency and cash-flow risks [1]
application_max_2: Furniture World pricing about 20% below Oxmoor's $950 sets and closing two local shops
$30,000 member fee for a share of a $500,000 budget at 3 European trade fairs
analysis_max_2: Shared marketing could lift output above 4,200 sets and defend revenue at home and abroad
Standards, currency and weak trade-fair results could waste fees and strain 85 workers
evaluation_max_2: Join the co-operative as a realistic route to export
Weighs modest fee against threat to home revenue and execution risks

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Saltwick Shrimp Co is a private limited company fishing and shelling shrimp off the coast of Country X near the town of Port Saffron. It employs 44 fishermen and 18 shellers, catching 900 tonnes a year sold at $5.20 per kilogram to domestic processors, earning about $4.68 million. Port Saffron unemployment stands at 13%.

Pelagia Seafood Group, a multinational company operating in 16 countries, has offered to build a $9 million processing plant in Port Saffron within 18 months. It would buy 600 tonnes of shrimp a year from Saltwick at $5.80 per kilogram and employ 220 local people, but wants Saltwick to stop supplying domestic processors. Its owners are abroad and say profits will be reinvested worldwide. The directors must decide whether to accept.

questions.question_text: Define 'tariff'.
questions.model_answer: A tariff is a tax placed by a government on imported goods, usually charged as a percentage of their value, to protect domestic firms or raise revenue. [2].

knowledge_max_2: A tax on imported goods [1]
Used to protect domestic firms / raise government revenue [1]

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits a multinational company can bring to a host country such as Port Saffron.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Multinationals create jobs in host countries. [k] Pelagia's plant would employ 220 local people where Port Saffron unemployment stands at 13%. [app] Reason 2: Multinationals bring capital investment into the host economy. [k] The $9 million processing plant would modernise the local seafood industry and bring new technology within 18 months. [app]

knowledge_max_2: Multinationals create employment in host countries [1]
Multinationals bring capital investment / new technology [1]
application_max_2: 220 local people employed in Port Saffron where unemployment is 13%
$9 million processing plant built within 18 months

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for stakeholders if Saltwick accepts Pelagia's offer.
questions.model_answer: Point 1: Saltwick would become dependent on a single powerful buyer. [k] Pelagia wants 600 of the 900 tonnes caught each year and wants Saltwick to stop supplying domestic processors. [app] If Pelagia later cut prices or cancelled orders, Saltwick could lose two-thirds of its market overnight. [an] Point 2: Local processors would lose their raw material supply. [k] Cutting off domestic processors would leave them short of shrimp. [app] Local processors could be forced to scale down or close, costing Country X jobs and reducing supply and choice for consumers. [an]

knowledge_max_2: Dependence on one powerful buyer weakens a supplier's bargaining position [1]
Diverting supply away from local customers harms those customers and consumers [1]
application_max_2: Pelagia wants 600 of 900 tonnes a year and an end to supplying domestic processors
$5.80 per kilogram offered vs $5.20 domestic
analysis_max_2: Two-thirds of volume lost at once if Pelagia squeezes terms, threatening viability
Processor closures reduce jobs and consumer choice in Country X

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltwick should accept Pelagia's offer? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Accepting would strengthen Saltwick's finances and Port Saffron's economy. [k] Pelagia would pay $5.80 per kilogram, about 60 cents above the domestic price, adding roughly $360,000 a year on 600 tonnes. [app] The $9 million plant would create 220 jobs for a town with 13% unemployment and guarantee demand for most of Saltwick's catch. [an] However, Saltwick would trade away its independence and loyal customers. [k] Supplying 600 of 900 tonnes to one buyer and abandoning domestic processors would leave Saltwick exposed if Pelagia drove prices down or withdrew. [app] Profits flowing abroad, possible pressure on fish stocks and lost goodwill with domestic customers could damage Port Saffron more than the jobs help. [an] Overall, Saltwick should accept only with safeguards, such as a minimum-price clause, a volume cap to protect stocks and keeping some supply for domestic processors. [eval] On balance, the extra $360,000 a year and 220 local jobs favour the deal, provided the contract protects Saltwick and the community rather than Pelagia alone. [eval]

knowledge_max_2: Accepting can secure revenue, jobs and investment for a host community [1]
Accepting can cost a firm its independence, customers and negotiating power [1]
application_max_2: $5.80 vs $5.20 per kilogram, about $360,000 extra a year on 600 tonnes
600 of 900 tonnes to one buyer; 220 jobs in a town with 13% unemployment
analysis_max_2: Guaranteed volume and price lift stabilise revenue and fund growth
Dependence on one buyer, profit repatriation and stock pressure threaten long-term interests
evaluation_max_2: Accept with contractual safeguards (minimum price, caps, retained domestic supply)
Weighs short-term revenue/jobs against independence, community and environmental risks
